title: Counting Numbers
snippet: Counting Numbers: The counting numbers start with 1 and continue. 1,2,3,4, \text{5…}
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Counting Numbers" title="Counting Numbers">
    <paragraph>The counting numbers start with $$1$$ and continue.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$1,2,3,4, \text{5…}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Whole Numbers
snippet: Whole Numbers: The whole numbers are the counting numbers and zero. 0,1,2,3,4, \text{5…}
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Whole Numbers" title="Whole Numbers">
    <paragraph>The whole numbers are the counting numbers and zero.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$0,1,2,3,4, \text{5…}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1.1
snippet: Example 1.1: Which of the following are ⓐ counting numbers? ⓑ whole numbers? 0,\frac{1}{4},3,5.2,15,105 ⓐ The counting numbers start at 1, so 0 is not a counting number. The numbers 3,15, \text{and} 105 are all counting numbers. ⓑ Whole...
body_xml:
<example number="1.1">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which of the following are ⓐ counting numbers? ⓑ whole numbers?</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$0,\frac{1}{4},3,5.2,15,105$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ The counting numbers start at $$1,$$ so $$0$$ is not a counting number. The numbers $$3,15, \text{and} 105$$ are all counting numbers.</item>
        <item>ⓑ Whole numbers are counting numbers and $$0.$$ The numbers $$0,3,15, \text{and} 105$$ are whole numbers.</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>The numbers $$\frac{1}{4}$$ and $$5.2$$ are neither counting numbers nor whole numbers. We will discuss these numbers later.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 1.3
snippet: Example 1.3: In the number 63,407,218; find the place value of each of the following digits: ⓐ 7 ⓑ 0 ⓒ 1 ⓓ 6 ⓔ 3 Write the number in a place value chart, starting at the right. ⓐ The 7 is in the thousands place. ⓑ The 0 is in the ten...
body_xml:
<example number="1.3">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In the number $$63,407,218;$$ find the place value of each of the following digits:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$7$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$0$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$1$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$6$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$3$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Write the number in a place value chart, starting at the right.</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ The $$7$$ is in the thousands place.</item>
        <item>ⓑ The $$0$$ is in the ten thousands place.</item>
        <item>ⓒ The $$1$$ is in the tens place.</item>
        <item>ⓓ The $$6$$ is in the ten millions place.</item>
        <item>ⓔ The $$3$$ is in the millions place.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Name a whole number in words. Step 1. Starting at the digit on the left, name the number in each period, followed by the period name. Do not include the period name for the ones. Step 2. Use commas in the number to separate the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Name a whole number in words.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Starting at the digit on the left, name the number in each period, followed by the period name. Do not include the period name for the ones.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Use commas in the number to separate the periods.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1.4
snippet: Example 1.4: Name the number 8,165,432,098,710 in words. Begin with the leftmost digit, which is 8. It is in the trillions place. eight trillion The next period to the right is billions. one hundred sixty-five billion The next period to...
body_xml:
Name the number $$8,165,432,098,710$$ in words. Begin with the leftmost digit, which is 8. It is in the trillions place. eight trillion The next period to the right is billions. one hundred sixty-five billion The next period to the right is millions. four hundred thirty-two million The next period to the right is thousands. ninety-eight thousand The rightmost period shows the ones. seven hundred ten
Putting all of the words together, we write $$8,165,432,098,710$$ as eight trillion, one hundred sixty-five billion, four hundred thirty-two million, ninety-eight thousand, seven hundred ten.

title: Example 1.5
snippet: Example 1.5: A student conducted research and found that the number of mobile phone users in the United States during one month in 2014 was 327,577,529. Name that number in words. Identify the periods associated with the number. Name the...
body_xml:
<example number="1.5">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A student conducted research and found that the number of mobile phone users in the United States during one month in $$2014$$ was $$327,577,529.$$ Name that number in words.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Identify the periods associated with the number.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Name the number in each period, followed by the period name. Put the commas in to separate the periods.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Millions period: three hundred twenty-seven million</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thousands period: five hundred seventy-seven thousand</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Ones period: five hundred twenty-nine</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So the number of mobile phone users in the Unites States during the month of April was three hundred twenty-seven million, five hundred seventy-seven thousand, five hundred twenty-nine.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Use place value to write a whole number. Step 1. Identify the words that indicate periods. (Remember the ones period is never named.) Step 2. Draw three blanks to indicate the number of places needed in each period. Separate the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Use place value to write a whole number.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Identify the words that indicate periods. (Remember the ones period is never named.)</item>
      <item>Step 2. Draw three blanks to indicate the number of places needed in each period. Separate the periods by commas.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Name the number in each period and place the digits in the correct place value position.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1.6
snippet: Example 1.6: Write the following numbers using digits. ⓐ fifty-three million, four hundred one thousand, seven hundred forty-two ⓑ nine billion, two hundred forty-six million, seventy-three thousand, one hundred eighty-nine ⓐ Identify the...
body_xml:
<example number="1.6">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the following numbers using digits.</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ fifty-three million, four hundred one thousand, seven hundred forty-two</item>
        <item>ⓑ nine billion, two hundred forty-six million, seventy-three thousand, one hundred eighty-nine</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ Identify the words that indicate periods.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Except for the first period, all other periods must have three places. Draw three blanks to indicate the number of places needed in each period. Separate the periods by commas.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then write the digits in each period.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Put the numbers together, including the commas. The number is $$53,401,742.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ Identify the words that indicate periods.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Except for the first period, all other periods must have three places. Draw three blanks to indicate the number of places needed in each period. Separate the periods by commas.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then write the digits in each period.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The number is $$9,246,073,189.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that in part ⓑ , a zero was needed as a place-holder in the hundred thousands place. Be sure to write zeros as needed to make sure that each period, except possibly the first, has three places.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 1.7
snippet: Example 1.7: A state budget was about $$\text{\$77} billion. Write the budget in standard form. Identify the periods. In this case, only two digits are given and they are in the billions period. To write the entire number, write zeros for...
body_xml:
<example number="1.7">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A state budget was about $$\text{\$77}$$ billion. Write the budget in standard form.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Identify the periods. In this case, only two digits are given and they are in the billions period. To write the entire number, write zeros for all of the other periods.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So the budget was about $$\text{\$77,000,000,000.}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Round a whole number to a specific place value. Step 1. Locate the given place value. All digits to the left of that place value do not change unless the given place value is a 9, in which case it may. (See Step 3.) Step 2....
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Round a whole number to a specific place value.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Locate the given place value. All digits to the left of that place value do not change unless the given place value is a 9, in which case it may. (See Step 3.)</item>
      <item>Step 2. Underline the digit to the right of the given place value.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Determine if this digit is greater than or equal to $$5.$$ Yes—add $$1$$ to the digit in the given place value. If that digit is 9, replace it with 0 and add 1 to the digit immediately to its left. If that digit is also a 9, repeat. No—do not change the digit in the given place value.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Replace all digits to the right of the given place value with zeros.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1.8
snippet: Example 1.8: Round 843 to the nearest ten. Locate the tens place. Underline the digit to the right of the tens place. Since 3 is less than 5, do not change the digit in the tens place. Replace all digits to the right of the tens place with...
body_xml: Round $$843$$ to the nearest ten. Locate the tens place. Underline the digit to the right of the tens place. Since 3 is less than 5, do not change the digit in the tens place. Replace all digits to the right of the tens place with zeros. Rounding 843 to the nearest ten gives 840.

title: Example 1.9
snippet: Example 1.9: Round each number to the nearest hundred: ⓐ 23,658 ⓑ 3,978 ⓐ Locate the hundreds place. The digit to the right of the hundreds place is 5. Underline the digit to the right of the hundreds place. Since 5 is greater than or...
body_xml:
Round each number to the nearest hundred: ⓐ $$23,658$$ ⓑ $$3,978$$ ⓐ Locate the hundreds place. The digit to the right of the hundreds place is 5. Underline the digit to the right of the hundreds place. Since 5 is greater than or equal to 5, round up by adding 1 to the digit in the hundreds place. Then replace all digits to the right of the hundreds place with zeros. So 23,658 rounded to the nearest hundred is 23,700.
ⓑ Locate the hundreds place. Underline the digit to the right of the hundreds place. The digit to the right of the hundreds place is 7. Since 7 is greater than or equal to 5, round up by adding 1 to the 9. Then place all digits to the right of the hundreds place with zeros. So 3,978 rounded to the nearest hundred is 4,000.

title: Example 1.10
snippet: Example 1.10: Round each number to the nearest thousand: ⓐ 147,032 ⓑ 29,504 ⓐ Locate the thousands place. Underline the digit to the right of the thousands place. The digit to the right of the thousands place is 0. Since 0 is less than 5,...
body_xml:
Round each number to the nearest thousand: ⓐ $$147,032$$ ⓑ $$29,504$$ ⓐ Locate the thousands place. Underline the digit to the right of the thousands place. The digit to the right of the thousands place is 0. Since 0 is less than 5, we do not change the digit in the thousands place. We then replace all digits to the right of the thousands pace with zeros. So 147,032 rounded to the nearest thousand is 147,000.
ⓑ Locate the thousands place. Underline the digit to the right of the thousands place. The digit to the right of the thousands place is 5. Since 5 is greater than or equal to 5, round up by adding 1 to the 9. Then replace all digits to the right of the thousands place with zeros. So 29,504 rounded to the nearest thousand is 30,000.
Notice that in part ⓑ , when we add $$1$$ thousand to the $$9$$ thousands, the total is $$10$$ thousands. We regroup this as $$1$$ ten thousand and $$0$$ thousands. We add the $$1$$ ten thousand to the $$2$$ ten thousands and put a $$0$$ in the thousands place.

title: Example 1.11
snippet: Example 1.11: Translate from math notation to words: ⓐ 7 + 1 ⓑ 12 + 14 ⓐ The expression consists of a plus symbol connecting the addends 7 and 1. We read this as seven plus one. The result is the sum of seven and one. ⓑ The expression...
body_xml:
<example number="1.11">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Translate from math notation to words:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$7 + 1$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$12 + 14$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ The expression consists of a plus symbol connecting the addends 7 and 1. We read this as seven plus one. The result is the sum of seven and one.</item>
        <item>ⓑ The expression consists of a plus symbol connecting the addends 12 and 14. We read this as twelve plus fourteen. The result is the sum of twelve and fourteen.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 1.12
snippet: Example 1.12: Model the addition 2 + 6. 2 + 6 means the sum of 2 and 6 Each addend is less than 10, so we can use ones blocks. Model the first number with 2 blocks. Model the second number with 6 blocks. Count the total number of blocks...
body_xml: Model the addition $$2 + 6.$$ $$2 + 6$$ means the sum of $$2$$ and $$6$$ Each addend is less than 10, so we can use ones blocks. Model the first number with 2 blocks. Model the second number with 6 blocks. Count the total number of blocks There are $$8$$ blocks in all, so $$2 + 6 = 8.$$

title: Example 1.13
snippet: Example 1.13: Model the addition 5 + 8. 5 + 8 means the sum of 5 and 8. Each addend is less than 10, se we can use ones blocks. Model the first number with 5 blocks. Model the second number with 8 blocks. Count the result. There are more...
body_xml:
Model the addition $$5 + 8.$$ $$5 + 8$$ means the sum of $$5$$ and $$8.$$ Each addend is less than 10, se we can use ones blocks. Model the first number with 5 blocks. Model the second number with 8 blocks. Count the result. There are more than 10 blocks so we exchange 10 ones blocks for 1 tens rod. Now we have 1 ten and 3 ones, which is 13. 5 + 8 = 13
Notice that we can describe the models as ones blocks and tens rods, or we can simply say ones and tens. From now on, we will use the shorter version but keep in mind that they mean the same thing.

title: Example 1.14
snippet: Example 1.14: Model the addition: 17 + 26. 17 + 26 means the sum of 17 and 26. Model the 17. 1 ten and 7 ones Model the 26. 2 tens and 6 ones Combine. 3 tens and 13 ones Exchange 10 ones for 1 ten. 4 tens and 3 ones 40 + 3 = 43 We have...
body_xml: Model the addition: $$17 + 26.$$ $$17 + 26$$ means the sum of 17 and 26. Model the 17. 1 ten and 7 ones Model the 26. 2 tens and 6 ones Combine. 3 tens and 13 ones Exchange 10 ones for 1 ten. 4 tens and 3 ones $$40 + 3 = 43$$ We have shown that $$17 + 26 = 43$$

title: Identity Property of Addition
snippet: Identity Property of Addition: The sum of any number a and 0 is the number. \begin{matrix} \\ {a + 0 = a} \\ {0 + a = a} \end{matrix}
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Identity Property of Addition" title="Identity Property of Addition">
    <paragraph>The sum of any number $$a$$ and $$0$$ is the number.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \\ {a + 0 = a} \\ {0 + a = a} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1.15
snippet: Example 1.15: Find each sum: ⓐ 0 + 11 ⓑ 42 + 0 ⓐ The first addend is zero. The sum of any number and zero is the number. 0 + 11 = 11 ⓑ The second addend is zero. The sum of any number and zero is the number. 42 + 0 = 42
body_xml: Find each sum: ⓐ $$0 + 11$$ ⓑ $$42 + 0$$ ⓐ The first addend is zero. The sum of any number and zero is the number. $$0 + 11 = 11$$ ⓑ The second addend is zero. The sum of any number and zero is the number. $$42 + 0 = 42$$

title: Commutative Property of Addition
snippet: Commutative Property of Addition: Changing the order of the addends a and b does not change their sum. a + b = b + a
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Commutative Property of Addition" title="Commutative Property of Addition">
    <paragraph>Changing the order of the addends $$a$$ and $$b$$ does not change their sum.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a + b = b + a$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1.16
snippet: Example 1.16: Add: ⓐ 8 + 7 ⓑ 7 + 8 ⓐ Add. 8 + 7 15 ⓑ Add. 7 + 8 15 Did you notice that changing the order of the addends did not change their sum? We could have immediately known the sum from part ⓑ just by recognizing that the addends...
body_xml:
<example number="1.16">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Add:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$8 + 7$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$7 + 8$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ Add. $$8 + 7$$ $$15$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ Add. $$7 + 8$$ $$15$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>Did you notice that changing the order of the addends did not change their sum? We could have immediately known the sum from part ⓑ just by recognizing that the addends were the same as in part ⓐ , but in the reverse order. As a result, both sums are the same.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 1.17
snippet: Example 1.17: Add: 28 + 61. To add numbers with more than one digit, it is often easier to write the numbers vertically in columns. Write the numbers so the ones and tens digits line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} {28 } \\ \\ {\underset{...
body_xml: Add: $$28 + 61.$$ To add numbers with more than one digit, it is often easier to write the numbers vertically in columns. Write the numbers so the ones and tens digits line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} {28 } \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+61}} \end{array}$$ Then add the digits in each place value. Add the ones: $$8 + 1 = 9$$ Add the tens: $$2 + 6 = 8$$ $$\begin{array}{r} {28 } \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+61}} \\ {89 } \end{array}$$

title: How To
snippet: How To: Add whole numbers. Step 1. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Step 2. Add the digits in each place value. Work from right to left starting with the ones place. If a sum in a place value is more than 9, carry...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Add whole numbers.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Add the digits in each place value. Work from right to left starting with the ones place. If a sum in a place value is more than $$9,$$ carry to the next place value.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Continue adding each place value from right to left, adding each place value and carrying if needed.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1.18
snippet: Example 1.18: Add: 43 + 69. Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} {43 } \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+69}} \end{array} Add the digits in each place.Add the ones: 3 + 9 = 12 Write the 2 in the ones...
body_xml: Add: $$43 + 69.$$ Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} {43 } \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+69}} \end{array}$$ Add the digits in each place.Add the ones: $$3 + 9 = 12$$ Write the $$2$$ in the ones place in the sum.Add the $$1$$ ten to the tens place. $$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{1}{4}3}} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+69} \\ {2} \end{array}$$ Now add the tens: $$1 + 4 + 6 = 11$$ Write the 11 in the sum. $$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{1}{4}3}} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_} }{+69} \\ {112} \end{array}$$

title: Example 1.19
snippet: Example 1.19: Add: 324 + 586. Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. Add the digits in each place value.Add the ones: 4 + 6 = 10 Write the 0 in the ones place in the sum and carry the 1 ten to the tens place. Add the tens: 1 +...
body_xml: Add: $$324 + 586.$$ Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. Add the digits in each place value.Add the ones: $$4 + 6 = 10$$ Write the $$0$$ in the ones place in the sum and carry the $$1$$ ten to the tens place. Add the tens: $$1 + 2 + 8 = 11$$ Write the $$1$$ in the tens place in the sum and carry the $$1$$ hundred to the hundreds Add the hundreds: $$1 + 3 + 5 = 9$$ Write the $$9$$ in the hundreds place.

title: Example 1.20
snippet: Example 1.20: Add: 1,683 + 479. Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} {1,683 } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \end{array} Add the digits in each place value. Add the ones: 3 + 9 = 12. Write...
body_xml:
Add: $$1,683 + 479.$$ Write the numbers so the digits line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} {1,683 } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \end{array}$$ Add the digits in each place value. Add the ones: $$3 + 9 = 12.$$ Write the $$2$$ in the ones place of the sum and carry the $$1$$ ten to the tens place. $$\begin{array}{r} {{1,6\overset{1}{8}3} } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \\ {2 } \end{array}$$ Add the tens: $$1 + 7 + 8 = 16$$ Write the $$6$$ in the tens place and carry the $$1$$ hundred to the hundreds place. $$\begin{array}{r} {{1,\overset{1}{6}\overset{1}{8}3} } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \\ {62 } \end{array}$$ Add the hundreds: $$1 + 6 + 4 = 11$$ Write the $$1$$ in the hundreds place and carry the $$1$$ thousand to the thousands place. $$\begin{array}{r} {{1,\overset{1}{6}\overset{1}{8}3} } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \\ {162 } \end{array}$$ Add the thousands $$1 + 1 = 2$$ .Write the $$2$$ in the thousands place of the sum. $$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{1}{1,}\overset{1}{6}\overset{1}{8}3} } \\ \\ { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \\ {2,162 } \end{array}$$
When the addends have different numbers of digits, be careful to line up the corresponding place values starting with the ones and moving toward the left.

title: Example 1.21
snippet: Example 1.21: Add: 21,357 + 861 + 8,596. Write the numbers so the place values line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} 21,357 \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \end{array} Add the digits in each place value. Add the...
body_xml:
Add: $$21,357 + 861 + 8,596.$$ Write the numbers so the place values line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} 21,357 \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \end{array}$$ Add the digits in each place value. Add the ones: $$7 + 1 + 6 = 14$$ Write the $$4$$ in the ones place of the sum and carry the $$1$$ to the tens place. $$\begin{array}{r} {21,3\overset{1}{5}7} \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \\ 4 \end{array}$$ Add the tens: $$1 + 5 + 6 + 9 = 21$$ Write the $$1$$ in the tens place and carry the $$2$$ to the hundreds place. $$\begin{array}{r} {21,\overset{2}{3}\overset{1}{5}7} \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \\ 14 \end{array}$$ Add the hundreds: $$2 + 3 + 8 + 5 = 18$$ Write the $$8$$ in the hundreds place and carry the $$1$$ to the thousands place. $$\begin{array}{r} {2\overset{1}{1,}\overset{2}{3}\overset{1}{5}7} \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \\ 814 \end{array}$$ Add the thousands $$1 + 1 + 8 = 10$$ .Write the $$0$$ in the thousands place and carry the $$1$$ to the ten thousands place. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{1}{2}\overset{1}{1,}\overset{2}{3}\overset{1}{5}7} \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \\ 0814 \end{array}$$ Add the ten-thousands $$1 + 2 = 3$$ .Write the $$3$$ in the ten thousands place in the sum. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{1}{2}\overset{1}{1,}\overset{2}{3}\overset{1}{5}7} \\ 861 \\ \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 8,596}} \\ 30,814 \end{array}$$
This example had three addends. We can add any number of addends using the same process as long as we are careful to line up the place values correctly.

title: Example 1.22
snippet: Example 1.22: Translate and simplify: the sum of 19 and 23. The word sum tells us to add. The words of 19 and 23 tell us the addends. The sum of 19 and 23 Translate. 19 + 23 Add. 42 The sum of 19 and 23 is 42.
body_xml: Translate and simplify: the sum of $$19$$ and $$23.$$ The word sum tells us to add. The words of $$19$$ and $$23$$ tell us the addends. The sum of $$19$$ and $$23$$ Translate. $$19 + 23$$ Add. $$42$$ The sum of $$19$$ and $$23$$ is $$42.$$

title: Example 1.23
snippet: Example 1.23: Translate and simplify: 28 increased by 31. The words increased by tell us to add. The numbers given are the addends. 28 increased by 31. Translate. 28 + 31 Add. 59 So 28 increased by 31 is 59.

title: Example 1.24

title: Example 1.32
snippet: Example 1.32: Subtract: 43 - 26. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. We cannot subtract 6 from 3, so we borrow 1 ten. This makes 3 tens and 13 ones. We write these numbers above each place and...
body_xml: Subtract: $$43 - 26.$$ Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. We cannot subtract 6 from 3, so we borrow 1 ten. This makes 3 tens and 13 ones. We write these numbers above each place and cross out the original digits. Now we can subtract the ones. $$13 - 6 = 7.$$ We write the 7 in the ones place in the difference. Now we subtract the tens. $$3 - 2 = 1.$$ We write the 1 in the tens place in the difference. Check by adding. Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.33
snippet: Example 1.33: Subtract and then check by adding: 207 - 64. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. 7 - 4 = 3. Write the 3 in the ones place in the difference. Subtract the tens. We cannot subtract 6...
body_xml: Subtract and then check by adding: $$207 - 64.$$ Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. $$7 - 4 = 3.$$ Write the 3 in the ones place in the difference. Subtract the tens. We cannot subtract 6 from 0 so we borrow 1 hundred and add 10 tens to the 0 tens we had. This makes a total of 10 tens. We write 10 above the tens place and cross out the 0. Then we cross out the 2 in the hundreds place and write 1 above it. Now we subtract the tens. $$10 - 6 = 4.$$ We write the 4 in the tens place in the difference. Finally, subtract the hundreds. There is no digit in the hundreds place in the bottom number so we can imagine a 0 in that place. Since $$1 - 0 = 1,$$ we write 1 in the hundreds place in the difference. Check by adding. Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.34
snippet: Example 1.34: Subtract and then check by adding: 910 - 586. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. We cannot subtract 6 from 0, so we borrow 1 ten and add 10 ones to the 0 ones we had. This makes 10...
body_xml: Subtract and then check by adding: $$910 - 586.$$ Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. We cannot subtract 6 from 0, so we borrow 1 ten and add 10 ones to the 0 ones we had. This makes 10 ones. We write a 0 above the tens place and cross out the 1. We write the 10 above the ones place and cross out the 0. Now we can subtract the ones. $$10 - 6 = 4.$$ Write the 4 in the ones place of the difference. Subtract the tens. We cannot subtract 8 from 0, so we borrow 1 hundred and add 10 tens to the 0 tens we had, which gives us 10 tens. Write 8 above the hundreds place and cross out the 9. Write 10 above the tens place. Now we can subtract the tens. $$10 - 8 = 2$$ . Subtract the hundreds place. $$8 - 5 = 3$$ Write the 3 in the hundreds place in the difference. Check by adding. Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.35
snippet: Example 1.35: Subtract and then check by adding: 2,162 - 479. Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. Since we cannot subtract 9 from 2, borrow 1 ten and add 10 ones to the 2 ones to make 12 ones....
body_xml:
Subtract and then check by adding: $$2,162 - 479.$$ Write the numbers so each place value lines up vertically. Subtract the ones. Since we cannot subtract 9 from 2, borrow 1 ten and add 10 ones to the 2 ones to make 12 ones. Write 5 above the tens place and cross out the 6. Write 12 above the ones place and cross out the 2. Now we can subtract the ones. $$12 - 9 = 3$$ Write 3 in the ones place in the difference. Subtract the tens. Since we cannot subtract 7 from 5, borrow 1 hundred and add 10 tens to the 5 tens to make 15 tens. Write 0 above the hundreds place and cross out the 1. Write 15 above the tens place. Now we can subtract the tens. $$15 - 7 = 8$$ Write 8 in the tens place in the difference. Now we can subtract the hundreds. Write 6 in the hundreds place in the difference. Subtract the thousands. There is no digit in the thousands place of the bottom number, so we imagine a 0. $$1 - 0 = 1.$$ Write 1 in the thousands place of the difference. Check by adding. $$\begin{array}{l} \\ { \overset{1}{1},\overset{1}{6}\overset{1}{8}3} \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{+ 479}} \\ { 2, 162✓} \end{array}$$
Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.44
snippet: Example 1.44: Multiply: 15 \cdot 4. Write the numbers so the digits 5 and 4 line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} {15} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 4} \end{array} Multiply 4 by the digit in the ones place of 15. 4 \cdot 5 = 20....
body_xml: Multiply: $$15 \cdot 4.$$ Write the numbers so the digits $$5$$ and $$4$$ line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} {15} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 4} \end{array}$$ Multiply $$4$$ by the digit in the ones place of $$15.$$ $$4 \cdot 5 = 20.$$ Write $$0$$ in the ones place of the product and carry the $$2$$ tens. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{2}{1}5} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 4} \\ {0} \end{array}$$ Multiply $$4$$ by the digit in the tens place of $$15.$$ $$4 \cdot 1 = 4$$ .Add the $$2$$ tens we carried. $$4 + 2 = 6$$ . Write the $$6$$ in the tens place of the product. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{2}{1}5} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 4} \\ {60} \end{array}$$

title: Example 1.45
snippet: Example 1.45: Multiply: 286 \cdot 5. Write the numbers so the digits 5 and 6 line up vertically. \begin{array}{r} {286} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 5} \end{array} Multiply 5 by the digit in the ones place of 286. 5 \cdot 6 =...
body_xml: Multiply: $$286 \cdot 5.$$ Write the numbers so the digits $$5$$ and $$6$$ line up vertically. $$\begin{array}{r} {286} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 5} \end{array}$$ Multiply $$5$$ by the digit in the ones place of $$286.$$ $$5 \cdot 6 = 30.$$ Write the $$0$$ in the ones place of the product and carry the $$3$$ to the tens place.Multiply $$5$$ by the digit in the tens place of $$286.$$ $$5 \cdot 8 = 40$$ . $$\begin{array}{r} \\ {2\overset{3}{8}6} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 5} \\ {0 } \end{array}$$ Add the $$3$$ tens we carried to get $$40 + 3 = 43$$ .Write the $$3$$ in the tens place of the product and carry the 4 to the hundreds place. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{4}{2}\overset{3}{8}6} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 5} \\ {30 } \end{array}$$ Multiply $$5$$ by the digit in the hundreds place of $$286.$$ $$5 \cdot 2 = 10.$$ Add the $$4$$ hundreds we carried to get $$10 + 4 = 14.$$ Write the $$4$$ in the hundreds place of the product and the $$1$$ to the thousands place. $$\begin{array}{r} {\overset{4}{2}\overset{3}{8}6} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 5} \\ {1,430 } \end{array}$$

title: Example 1.46
snippet: Example 1.46: Multiply: 62{(87)}. Write the numbers so each place lines up vertically. Start by multiplying 7 by 62. Multiply 7 by the digit in the ones place of 62. 7 \cdot 2 = 14. Write the 4 in the ones place of the product and carry...
body_xml:
Multiply: $$62{(87)}.$$ Write the numbers so each place lines up vertically. Start by multiplying 7 by 62. Multiply 7 by the digit in the ones place of 62. $$7 \cdot 2 = 14.$$ Write the 4 in the ones place of the product and carry the 1 to the tens place. Multiply 7 by the digit in the tens place of 62. $$7 \cdot 6 = 42.$$ Add the 1 ten we carried. $$42 + 1 = 43$$ . Write the 3 in the tens place of the product and the 4 in the hundreds place. The first partial product is 434. Now, write a 0 under the 4 in the ones place of the next partial product as a placeholder since we now multiply the digit in the tens place of 87 by 62. Multiply 8 by the digit in the ones place of 62. $$8 \cdot 2 = 16.$$ Write the 6 in the next place of the product, which is the tens place. Carry the 1 to the tens place. Multiply 8 by 6, the digit in the tens place of 62, then add the 1 ten we carried to get 49. Write the 9 in the hundreds place of the product and the 4 in the thousands place. The second partial product is 4960. Add the partial products.
The product is $$5,394.$$

Multiply: ⓐ $$47 \cdot 10$$ ⓑ $$47 \cdot 100.$$ ⓐ $$47 \cdot 10$$ . $$\begin{array}{r} {47} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_} }{\times 10} \\ 00 \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_} }{470} \\ 470 \end{array}$$ ⓑ $$47 \cdot 100$$ $$\begin{array}{r} {47 } \\ {\underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\times 100} } \\ {00} \\ \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_} }{\begin{array}{r} 000 \\ {4700} \end{array}} \\ {4,700 } \end{array}$$
When we multiplied $$47$$ times $$10,$$ the product was $$470.$$ Notice that $$10$$ has one zero, and we put one zero after $$47$$ to get the product. When we multiplied $$47$$ times $$100,$$ the product was $$4,700.$$ Notice that $$100$$ has two zeros and we put two zeros after $$47$$ to get the product. Do you see the pattern? If we multiplied $$47$$ times $$10,000,$$ which has four zeros, we would put four zeros after $$47$$ to get the product $$470,000.$$

title: How To
snippet: How To: Divide whole numbers. Step 1. Divide the first digit of the dividend by the divisor. If the divisor is larger than the first digit of the dividend, divide the first two digits of the dividend by the divisor, and so on. Step 2....
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Divide whole numbers.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Divide the first digit of the dividend by the divisor. If the divisor is larger than the first digit of the dividend, divide the first two digits of the dividend by the divisor, and so on.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Write the quotient above the dividend.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Multiply the quotient by the divisor and write the product under the dividend.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Subtract that product from the dividend.</item>
      <item>Step 5. Bring down the next digit of the dividend.</item>
      <item>Step 6. Repeat from Step 1 until there are no more digits in the dividend to bring down.</item>
      <item>Step 7. Check by multiplying the quotient times the divisor.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1.61
snippet: Example 1.61: Divide 2,596 \div 4. Check by multiplying: Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. Divide the first digit of the dividend, 2, by the divisor, 4. Since 4 does not go into 2, we use the first two digits of the...
body_xml:
Divide $$2,596 \div 4.$$ Check by multiplying: Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. Divide the first digit of the dividend, 2, by the divisor, 4. Since 4 does not go into 2, we use the first two digits of the dividend and divide 25 by 4. The divisor 4 goes into 25 six times. We write the 6 in the quotient above the 5. Multiply the 6 in the quotient by the divisor 4 and write the product, 24, under the first two digits in the dividend. Subtract that product from the first two digits in the dividend. Subtract $$25 - 24$$ . Write the difference, 1, under the second digit in the dividend. Now bring down the 9 and repeat these steps. There are 4 fours in 19. Write the 4 over the 9. Multiply the 4 by 4 and subtract this product from 19. Bring down the 6 and repeat these steps. There are 9 fours in 36. Write the 9 over the 6. Multiply the 9 by 4 and subtract this product from 36. So $$2,596 \div 4 = 649$$ . Check by multiplying.
It equals the dividend, so our answer is correct.

Since that won't work, we try 6 into 45.There are 7 sixes in 45. We write the 7 over the 5. Multiply the 7 by 6 and subtract this product from 45. Now bring down the 0 and repeat these steps. There are 5 sixes in 30.Write the 5 over the 0. Multiply the 5 by 6 and subtract this product from 30. Now bring down the 6 and repeat these steps. There is 1 six in 6. Write the 1 over the 6. Multiply 1 by 6 and subtract this product from 6. Check by multiplying.
It equals the dividend, so our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.63
snippet: Example 1.63: Divide 7,263 \div 9. Check by multiplying. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. First we try to divide 9 into 7. Since that won't work, we try 9 into 72. There are 8 nines in 72. We write the 8 over the...
body_xml:
Divide $$7,263 \div 9.$$ Check by multiplying. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. First we try to divide 9 into 7. Since that won't work, we try 9 into 72. There are 8 nines in 72. We write the 8 over the 2. Multiply the 8 by 9 and subtract this product from 72. Now bring down the 6 and repeat these steps. There are 0 nines in 6. Write the 0 over the 6. Multiply the 0 by 9 and subtract this product from 6. Now bring down the 3 and repeat these steps. There are 7 nines in 63. Write the 7 over the 3. Multiply the 7 by 9 and subtract this product from 63. Check by multiplying.
It equals the dividend, so our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.64
snippet: Example 1.64: Divide 1,439 \div 4. Check by multiplying. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. First we try to divide 4 into 1. Since that won't work, we try 4 into 14. There are 3 fours in 14. We write the 3 over the...
body_xml:
Divide $$1,439 \div 4.$$ Check by multiplying. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. First we try to divide 4 into 1. Since that won't work, we try 4 into 14. There are 3 fours in 14. We write the 3 over the 4. Multiply the 3 by 4 and subtract this product from 14. Now bring down the 3 and repeat these steps. There are 5 fours in 23. Write the 5 over the 3. Multiply the 5 by 4 and subtract this product from 23. Now bring down the 9 and repeat these steps. There are 9 fours in 39. Write the 9 over the 9. Multiply the 9 by 4 and subtract this product from 39. There are no more numbers to bring down, so we are done. The remainder is 3. Check by multiplying.
So $$1,439 \div 4$$ is $$359$$ with a remainder of $$3.$$ Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.65
snippet: Example 1.65: Divide and then check by multiplying: 1,461 \div 13. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. 131,461 First we try to divide 13 into 1. Since that won't work, we try 13 into 14. There is 1 thirteen in 14. We...
body_xml:
Divide and then check by multiplying: $$1,461 \div 13.$$ Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. $$131,461$$ First we try to divide 13 into 1. Since that won't work, we try 13 into 14. There is 1 thirteen in 14. We write the 1 over the 4. Multiply the 1 by 13 and subtract this product from 14. Now bring down the 6 and repeat these steps. There is 1 thirteen in 16. Write the 1 over the 6. Multiply the 1 by 13 and subtract this product from 16. Now bring down the 1 and repeat these steps. There are 2 thirteens in 31. Write the 2 over the 1. Multiply the 2 by 13 and subtract this product from 31. There are no more numbers to bring down, so we are done. The remainder is 5. $$1,462 \div 13$$ is 112 with a remainder of 5. Check by multiplying.
Our answer is correct.

title: Example 1.66
snippet: Example 1.66: Divide and check by multiplying: 74,521 \div 241. Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. 24174,521 First we try to divide 241 into 7. Since that won’t work, we try 241 into 74. That still won’t work, so we...
body_xml:
Divide and check by multiplying: $$74,521 \div 241.$$ Let's rewrite the problem to set it up for long division. $$24174,521$$ First we try to divide 241 into 7. Since that won’t work, we try 241 into 74. That still won’t work, so we try 241 into 745. Since 2 divides into 7 three times, we try 3. Since $$3 \times 241 = 723$$ , we write the 3 over the 5 in 745. Note that 4 would be too large because $$4 \times 241 = 964$$ , which is greater than 745. Multiply the 3 by 241 and subtract this product from 745. Now bring down the 2 and repeat these steps. 241 does not divide into 222. We write a 0 over the 2 as a placeholder and then continue. Now bring down the 1 and repeat these steps. Try 9. Since $$9 \times 241 = 2,169$$ , we write the 9 over the 1. Multiply the 9 by 241 and subtract this product from 2,221. There are no more numbers to bring down, so we are finished. The remainder is 52. So $$74,521 \div 241$$ is 309 with a remainder of 52. Check by multiplying.
Sometimes it might not be obvious how many times the divisor goes into digits of the dividend. We will have to guess and check numbers to find the greatest number that goes into the digits without exceeding them.

title: Order of Operations
snippet: Order of Operations: When simplifying mathematical expressions perform the operations in the following order: 1. Parentheses and other Grouping Symbols Simplify all expressions inside the parentheses or other grouping symbols, working on...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Order of Operations" title="Order of Operations">
    <paragraph>When simplifying mathematical expressions perform the operations in the following order:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>1. Parentheses and other Grouping Symbols</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Simplify all expressions inside the parentheses or other grouping symbols, working on the innermost parentheses first.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>2. Exponents</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Simplify all expressions with exponents.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>3. Multiplication and Division</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Perform all multiplication and division in order from left to right. These operations have equal priority.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>4. Addition and Subtraction</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Perform all addition and subtraction in order from left to right. These operations have equal priority.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 2.11
snippet: Example 2.11: \text{Simplify:} {5 + 2^{3}} + 3\left\lbrack {6 - 3(4 - 2)} \right\rbrack. Are there any parentheses (or other grouping symbol)? Yes. Focus on the parentheses that are inside the brackets. Subtract. Continue inside the...
body_xml: $$\text{Simplify:} {5 + 2^{3}} + 3\left\lbrack {6 - 3(4 - 2)} \right\rbrack.$$ Are there any parentheses (or other grouping symbol)? Yes. Focus on the parentheses that are inside the brackets. Subtract. Continue inside the brackets and multiply. Continue inside the brackets and subtract. The expression inside the brackets requires no further simplification. Are there any exponents? Yes. Simplify exponents. Is there any multiplication or division? Yes. Multiply. Is there any addition or subtraction? Yes. Add. Add.

title: Example 2.13
snippet: Example 2.13: Evaluate x + 7 when ⓐ x = 3 ⓑ x = 12 ⓐ To evaluate, substitute 3 for x in the expression, and then simplify. Substitute. Add. When x = 3, the expression x + 7 has a value of 10. ⓑ To evaluate, substitute 12 for x in the...
body_xml:
Evaluate $$x + 7$$ when ⓐ $$x = 3$$ ⓑ $$x = 12$$ ⓐ To evaluate, substitute $$3$$ for $$x$$ in the expression, and then simplify. Substitute. Add.
When $$x = 3,$$ the expression $$x + 7$$ has a value of $$10.$$ ⓑ To evaluate, substitute $$12$$ for $$x$$ in the expression, and then simplify. Substitute. Add.
When $$x = 12,$$ the expression $$x + 7$$ has a value of $$19.$$ Notice that we got different results for parts ⓐ and ⓑ even though we started with the same expression. This is because the values used for $$x$$ were different. When we evaluate an expression, the value varies depending on the value used for the variable.

title: Example 2.14
snippet: Example 2.14: Evaluate 9x - 2, \text{when} \ ⓐ x = 5 \ ⓑ x = 1 Remember ab means a times b, so 9x means 9 times x. ⓐ To evaluate the expression when x = 5, we substitute 5 for x, and then simplify. Multiply. Subtract. ⓑ To evaluate the...
body_xml:

ⓑ To evaluate the expression when $$x = 1,$$ we substitute $$1$$ for $$x,$$ and then simplify. Multiply. Subtract.
Notice that in part ⓐ that we wrote $$9 \cdot 5$$ and in part ⓑ we wrote $$9(1).$$ Both the dot and the parentheses tell us to multiply.

snippet: Example 2.17: \text{Evaluate} 3x + 4y - 6 \text{when} x = 10 \text{and} y = 2. This expression contains two variables, so we must make two substitutions. Multiply. Add and subtract left to right. When x = 10 and y = 2, the expression 3x +...
body_xml:

title: Example 2.19
snippet: Example 2.19: Identify each term in the expression 9b + 15x^{2} + a + 6. Then identify the coefficient of each term. The expression has four terms. They are 9b,15x^{2},a, and 6. The coefficient of 9b is 9. The coefficient of 15x^{2} is 15....

<example number="2.19">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify each term in the expression $$9b + 15x^{2} + a + 6.$$ Then identify the coefficient of each term.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The expression has four terms. They are $$9b,15x^{2},a,$$ and $$6.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coefficient of $$9b$$ is $$9.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coefficient of $$15x^{2}$$ is $$15.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Remember that if no number is written before a variable, the coefficient is $$1.$$ So the coefficient of $$a$$ is $$1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coefficient of a constant is the constant, so the coefficient of $$6$$ is $$6.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Like Terms
snippet: Like Terms: Terms that are either constants or have the same variables with the same exponents are like terms.

<note type="rule" source_type="Like Terms" title="Like Terms">
    <paragraph>Terms that are either constants or have the same variables with the same exponents are like terms.</paragraph>

title: Example 2.20
snippet: Example 2.20: Identify the like terms: ⓐ y^{3},7x^{2},14,23,4y^{3},9x,5x^{2} ⓑ 4x^{2} + 2x + 5x^{2} + 6x + 40x + 8xy ⓐ y^{3},7x^{2},14,23,4y^{3},9x,5x^{2} Look at the variables and exponents. The expression contains y^{3},x^{2},x, and...
body_xml:
<example number="2.20">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the like terms:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$y^{3},7x^{2},14,23,4y^{3},9x,5x^{2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$4x^{2} + 2x + 5x^{2} + 6x + 40x + 8xy$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$y^{3},7x^{2},14,23,4y^{3},9x,5x^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Look at the variables and exponents. The expression contains $$y^{3},x^{2},x,$$ and constants.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The terms $$y^{3}$$ and $$4y^{3}$$ are like terms because they both have $$y^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The terms $$7x^{2}$$ and $$5x^{2}$$ are like terms because they both have $$x^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The terms $$14$$ and $$23$$ are like terms because they are both constants.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The term $$9x$$ does not have any like terms in this list since no other terms have the variable $$x$$ raised to the power of $$1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ $$4x^{2} + 2x + 5x^{2} + 6x + 40x + 8xy$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Look at the variables and exponents. The expression contains the terms $$4x^{2},2x,5x^{2},6x,40x, \text{and} 8xy$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The terms $$4x^{2}$$ and $$5x^{2}$$ are like terms because they both have $$x^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The terms $$2x,6x, \text{and} 40x$$ are like terms because they all have $$x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The term $$8xy$$ has no like terms in the given expression because no other terms contain the two variables $$xy.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 2.23
snippet: Example 2.23: Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression: ⓐ the difference of 20 and 4 ⓑ the quotient of 10x and 3 ⓐ The key word is difference, which tells us the operation is subtraction. Look for the words of and and to...
body_xml:
<example number="2.23">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ the difference of $$20$$ and $$4$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ the quotient of $$10x$$ and $$3$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ The key word is difference, which tells us the operation is subtraction. Look for the words of and and to find the numbers to subtract.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} \\ { \text{the difference} \text{of} 20 and 4} \\ {20 \text{minus} 4} \\ {20 - 4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ The key word is quotient, which tells us the operation is division.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} \\ { \text{the quotient of} 10x \text{and} 3} \\ { \text{divide} 10x \text{by} 3} \\ {10x \div 3} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This can also be written as $$\begin{array}{l} {10x/3 \text{or} \frac{10x}{3}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 2.24
snippet: Example 2.24: Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression: ⓐ Eight more than y ⓑ Seven less than 9z ⓐ The key words are more than. They tell us the operation is addition. More than means “added to”. \begin{array}{l} {...
body_xml:
<example number="2.24">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ Eight more than $$y$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ Seven less than $$9z$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ The key words are more than. They tell us the operation is addition. More than means “added to”.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} { \text{Eight more than} y} \\ { \text{Eight added to} y} \\ {y + 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ The key words are less than. They tell us the operation is subtraction. Less than means “subtracted from”.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} { \text{Seven less than} 9z} \\ { \text{Seven subtracted from} 9z} \\ {9z - 7} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 2.25
snippet: Example 2.25: Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression: ⓐ five times the sum of m and n ⓑ the sum of five times m and n ⓐ There are two operation words: times tells us to multiply and sum tells us to add. Because we are...
body_xml:
<example number="2.25">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Translate each word phrase into an algebraic expression:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ five times the sum of $$m$$ and $$n$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ the sum of five times $$m$$ and $$n$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ There are two operation words: times tells us to multiply and sum tells us to add. Because we are multiplying $$5$$ times the sum, we need parentheses around the sum of $$m$$ and $$n.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>five times the sum of $$m$$ and $$n$$ $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ { 5\left( {m + n} \right)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ To take a sum, we look for the words of and and to see what is being added. Here we are taking the sum of five times $$m$$ and $$n.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>the sum of five times $$m$$ and $$n$$ $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ { 5{m + n}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice how the use of parentheses changes the result. In part ⓐ , we add first and in part ⓑ , we multiply first.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 2.26
snippet: Example 2.26: The height of a rectangular window is 6 inches less than the width. Let w represent the width of the window. Write an expression for the height of the window. Write a phrase about the height. 6 less than the width Substitute...

title: Example 2.27
snippet: Example 2.27: Blanca has dimes and quarters in her purse. The number of dimes is 2 less than 5 times the number of quarters. Let q represent the number of quarters. Write an expression for the number of dimes. Write a phrase about the...

title: Solution of an Equation
snippet: Solution of an Equation: A solution to an equation is a value of a variable that makes a true statement when substituted into the equation. The process of finding the solution to an equation is called solving the equation.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Solution of an Equation" title="Solution of an Equation">
    <paragraph>A solution to an equation is a value of a variable that makes a true statement when substituted into the equation.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The process of finding the solution to an equation is called solving the equation.</paragraph>
  </note>

unit_title: Solving Equations Using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality
title: How To
snippet: How To: Determine whether a number is a solution to an equation. Step 1. Substitute the number for the variable in the equation. Step 2. Simplify the expressions on both sides of the equation. Step 3. Determine whether the resulting...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Determine whether a number is a solution to an equation.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Substitute the number for the variable in the equation.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Simplify the expressions on both sides of the equation.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Determine whether the resulting equation is true. If it is true, the number is a solution. If it is not true, the number is not a solution.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 2.28
snippet: Example 2.28: \text{Determine whether} x = 5 \text{is a solution of} 6x - 17 = 16. Multiply. Subtract. So x = 5 is not a solution to the equation 6x - 17 = 16.
body_xml:
$$\text{Determine whether} x = 5 \text{is a solution of} 6x - 17 = 16.$$ Multiply. Subtract.
So $$x = 5$$ is not a solution to the equation $$6x - 17 = 16.$$

unit_title: Solving Equations Using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality
title: Example 2.29
snippet: Example 2.29: \text{Determine whether} y = 2 \text{is a solution of} 6y - 4 = 5y - 2. Here, the variable appears on both sides of the equation. We must substitute 2 for each y. Multiply. Subtract. Since y = 2 results in a true equation, we...
body_xml:
$$\text{Determine whether} y = 2 \text{is a solution of} 6y - 4 = 5y - 2.$$ Here, the variable appears on both sides of the equation. We must substitute $$2$$ for each $$y.$$ Multiply. Subtract.
Since $$y = 2$$ results in a true equation, we know that $$2$$ is a solution to the equation $$6y - 4 = 5y - 2.$$

title: Example 2.30
snippet: Example 2.30: Write an equation modeled by the envelopes and counters, and then solve the equation: On the left, write x for the contents of the envelope, add the 4 counters, so we have x + 4 . x + 4 On the right, there are 5 counters. 5...
body_xml:
Write an equation modeled by the envelopes and counters, and then solve the equation: On the left, write $$x$$ for the contents of the envelope, add the $$4$$ counters, so we have $$x + 4$$ . $$x + 4$$ On the right, there are $$5$$ counters. $$5$$ The two sides are equal. $$x + 4 = 5$$ Solve the equation by subtracting $$4$$ counters from each side.
We can see that there is one counter in the envelope. This can be shown algebraically as: Substitute $$1$$ for $$x$$ in the equation to check. Since $$x = 1$$ makes the statement true, we know that $$1$$ is indeed a solution.

snippet: Example 2.31: Solve: x + 8 = 17. We will use the Subtraction Property of Equality to isolate x. Subtract 8 from both sides. Simplify. Since x = 9 makes x + 8 = 17 a true statement, we know 9 is the solution to the equation.
body_xml:
Solve: $$x + 8 = 17.$$ We will use the Subtraction Property of Equality to isolate $$x.$$ Subtract 8 from both sides. Simplify.
Since $$x = 9$$ makes $$x + 8 = 17$$ a true statement, we know $$9$$ is the solution to the equation.

unit_title: Solving Equations Using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality
title: Example 2.32
snippet: Example 2.32: Solve: 100 = y + 74. To solve an equation, we must always isolate the variable—it doesn’t matter which side it is on. To isolate y, we will subtract 74 from both sides. Subtract 74 from both sides. Simplify. Substitute 26 for...
body_xml:
Solve: $$100 = y + 74.$$ To solve an equation, we must always isolate the variable—it doesn’t matter which side it is on. To isolate $$y,$$ we will subtract $$74$$ from both sides. Subtract 74 from both sides. Simplify. Substitute $$26$$ for $$y$$ to check.
Since $$y = 26$$ makes $$100 = y + 74$$ a true statement, we have found the solution to this equation.

snippet: Example 2.34: Solve: 27 = a - 16. We will add 16 to each side to isolate the variable. Add 16 to each side. Simplify. The solution to 27 = a - 16 is a = 43.
body_xml:

Determine whether each of the given numbers is a multiple of $$3:\$$ ⓐ $$645\$$ ⓑ $$10,519$$ ⓐ Is $$645$$ a multiple of $$3?$$ Find the sum of the digits. $$6 + 4 + 5 = 15$$ Is 15 a multiple of 3? Yes. If we're not sure, we could add its digits to find out. We can check it by dividing 645 by 3. $$645 \div 3$$ The quotient is 215. $$3 \cdot 215 = 645$$
ⓑ Is $$10,519$$ a multiple of $$3?$$ Find the sum of the digits. $$1 + 0 + 5 + 1 + 9 = 16$$ Is 16 a multiple of 3? No. So 10,519 is not a multiple of 3 either.. $$645 \div 3$$ We can check this by dividing by 10,519 by 3. $$\begin{matrix} {3,506 \text{R} 1} \\ {310,519 } \end{matrix}$$
When we divide $$10,519$$ by $$3,$$ we do not get a counting number, so $$10,519$$ is not the product of a counting number and $$3.$$ It is not a multiple of $$3.$$

    <list type="ordered">

<example number="2.46">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find all the factors of $$72.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Divide $$72$$ by each of the counting numbers starting with $$1.$$ If the quotient is a whole number, the divisor and quotient are a pair of factors.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The next line would have a divisor of $$9$$ and a quotient of $$8.$$ The quotient would be smaller than the divisor, so we stop. If we continued, we would end up only listing the same factors again in reverse order. Listing all the factors from smallest to greatest, we have</paragraph>

Identify each number as prime or composite: ⓐ $$83\$$ ⓑ $$77$$ ⓐ Test each prime, in order, to see if it is a factor of $$83$$ , starting with $$2,$$ as shown. We will stop when the quotient is smaller than the divisor. Prime Test Factor of $$83?$$ $$2$$ Last digit of $$83$$ is not $$0,2,4,6, \text{or} 8.$$ No. $$3$$ $$8 + 3 = 11,$$ and $$11$$ is not divisible by $$3.$$ No. $$5$$ The last digit of $$83$$ is not $$5$$ or $$0.$$ No. $$7$$ $$83 \div 7 = 11.857 \text{….}$$ No. $$11$$ $$83 \div 11 = 7.545 \text{…}$$ No.
We can stop when we get to $$11$$ because the quotient $$\text{(7.545…)}$$ is less than the divisor. We did not find any prime numbers that are factors of $$83,$$ so we know $$83$$ is prime. ⓑ Test each prime, in order, to see if it is a factor of $$77.$$ Prime Test Factor of $$77?$$ $$2$$ Last digit is not $$0,2,4,6, \text{or} 8.$$ No. $$3$$ $$7 + 7 = 14,$$ and $$14$$ is not divisible by $$3.$$ No. $$5$$ the last digit is not $$5$$ or $$0.$$ No. $$7$$ $$77 \div 7 = 11$$ Yes.
Since $$77$$ is divisible by $$7,$$ we know it is not a prime number. It is composite.

title: Absolute Value

snippet: Example 3.19: Simplify: ⓐ 19 + (-47) ⓑ -32 + 40 ⓐ Since the signs are different, we subtract 19 from 47. The answer will be negative because there are more negatives than positives. \begin{matrix} {19 + (-47)} \\ -28 \end{matrix} ⓑ The...
body_xml:
<example number="3.19">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$19 + (-47)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$-32 + 40$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ Since the signs are different, we subtract $$19$$ from $$47.$$ The answer will be negative because there are more negatives than positives.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {19 + (-47)} \\ -28 \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ The signs are different so we subtract $$32$$ from $$40.$$ The answer will be positive because there are more positives than negatives</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {-32 + 40} \\ 8 \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Example 4.1: Name the fraction of the shape that is shaded in each of the figures. We need to ask two questions. First, how many equal parts are there? This will be the denominator. Second, of these equal parts, how many are shaded? This...
body_xml:
<example number="4.1">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Name the fraction of the shape that is shaded in each of the figures.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We need to ask two questions. First, how many equal parts are there? This will be the denominator. Second, of these equal parts, how many are shaded? This will be the numerator.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{lccl} \text{How many equal parts are there?} & & & { \text{There are eight equal parts} .} \\ \text{How many are shaded?} & & & { \text{Five parts are shaded} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Five out of eight parts are shaded. Therefore, the fraction of the circle that is shaded is $$\frac{5}{8}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{lccl} \text{How many equal parts are there?} & & & { \text{There are nine equal parts} .} \\ \text{How many are shaded?} & & & { \text{Two parts are shaded} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Two out of nine parts are shaded. Therefore, the fraction of the square that is shaded is $$\frac{2}{9}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

<example number="4.13">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use fraction tiles to find equivalent fractions. Show your result with a figure.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ How many eighths equal one-half?</item>
        <item>ⓑ How many tenths equal one-half?</item>
        <item>ⓒ How many twelfths equal one-half?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ It takes four $$\frac{1}{8}$$ tiles to exactly cover the $$\frac{1}{2}$$ tile, so $$\frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ It takes five $$\frac{1}{10}$$ tiles to exactly cover the $$\frac{1}{2}$$ tile, so $$\frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒ It takes six $$\frac{1}{12}$$ tiles to exactly cover the $$\frac{1}{2}$$ tile, so $$\frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Suppose you had tiles marked $$\frac{1}{20}.$$ How many of them would it take to equal $$\frac{1}{2}?$$ Are you thinking ten tiles? If you are, you’re right, because $$\frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We have shown that $$\frac{1}{2},\frac{2}{4},\frac{3}{6},\frac{4}{8},\frac{5}{10},\frac{6}{12},$$ and $$\frac{10}{20}$$ are all equivalent fractions.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Example 4.16: Locate and label the following on a number line: \frac{3}{4},\frac{4}{3},\frac{5}{3},4\frac{1}{5}, and \frac{7}{2}. Start by locating the proper fraction \frac{3}{4}. It is between 0 and 1. To do this, divide the distance...

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start by locating the proper fraction $$\frac{3}{4}.$$ It is between $$0$$ and $$1.$$ To do this, divide the distance between $$0$$ and $$1$$ into four equal parts. Then plot $$\frac{3}{4}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, locate the mixed number $$4\frac{1}{5}.$$ It is between $$4$$ and $$5$$ on the number line. Divide the number line between $$4$$ and $$5$$ into five equal parts, and then plot $$4\frac{1}{5}$$ one-fifth of the way between $$4$$ and $$5$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now locate the improper fractions $$\frac{4}{3}$$ and $$\frac{5}{3}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>It is easier to plot them if we convert them to mixed numbers first.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{4}{3} = 1\frac{1}{3}, \frac{5}{3} = 1\frac{2}{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Divide the distance between $$1$$ and $$2$$ into thirds.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next let us plot $$\frac{7}{2}.$$ We write it as a mixed number, $$\frac{7}{2} = 3\frac{1}{2}$$ . Plot it between $$3$$ and $$4.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The number line shows all the numbers located on the number line.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 4.17
snippet: Example 4.17: Locate and label the following on the number line: \frac{1}{4}, - \frac{1}{4},1\frac{1}{3},-1\frac{1}{3},\frac{5}{2}, and - \frac{5}{2}. Draw a number line. Mark 0 in the middle and then mark several units to the left and...
body_xml:
<example number="4.17">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Locate and label the following on the number line: $$\frac{1}{4}, - \frac{1}{4},1\frac{1}{3},-1\frac{1}{3},\frac{5}{2},$$ and $$- \frac{5}{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Draw a number line. Mark $$0$$ in the middle and then mark several units to the left and right.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To locate $$\frac{1}{4},$$ divide the interval between $$0$$ and $$1$$ into four equal parts. Each part represents one-quarter of the distance. So plot $$\frac{1}{4}$$ at the first mark.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To locate $$- \frac{1}{4},$$ divide the interval between $$0$$ and $$-1$$ into four equal parts. Plot $$- \frac{1}{4}$$ at the first mark to the left of $$0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$1\frac{1}{3}$$ is between $$1$$ and $$2,$$ divide the interval between $$1$$ and $$2$$ into three equal parts. Plot $$1\frac{1}{3}$$ at the first mark to the right of $$1.$$ Then since $$-1\frac{1}{3}$$ is the opposite of $$1\frac{1}{3}$$ it is between $$-1$$ and $$-2.$$ Divide the interval between $$-1$$ and $$-2$$ into three equal parts. Plot $$-1\frac{1}{3}$$ at the first mark to the left of $$-1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To locate $$\frac{5}{2}$$ and $$- \frac{5}{2},$$ it may be helpful to rewrite them as the mixed numbers $$2\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$-2\frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$2\frac{1}{2}$$ is between $$2$$ and $$3,$$ divide the interval between $$2$$ and $$3$$ into two equal parts. Plot $$\frac{5}{2}$$ at the mark. Then since $$-2\frac{1}{2}$$ is between $$-2$$ and $$-3,$$ divide the interval between $$-2$$ and $$-3$$ into two equal parts. Plot $$- \frac{5}{2}$$ at the mark.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 4.37
snippet: Example 4.37: Multiply: 3\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8} 3\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8} Convert 3\frac{1}{3} to an improper fraction. \frac{10}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8} Multiply. \frac{10 \cdot 5}{3 \cdot 8} Look for common factors....
body_xml:
Multiply: $$3\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8}$$ $$3\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8}$$ Convert $$3\frac{1}{3}$$ to an improper fraction. $$\frac{10}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{8}$$ Multiply. $$\frac{10 \cdot 5}{3 \cdot 8}$$ Look for common factors. $$\frac{2\not{} \cdot 5 \cdot 5}{3 \cdot 2\not{} \cdot 4}$$ Remove common factors. $$\frac{5 \cdot 5}{3 \cdot 4}$$ Simplify. $$\frac{25}{12}$$
Notice that we left the answer as an improper fraction, $$\frac{25}{12},$$ and did not convert it to a mixed number. In algebra, it is preferable to write answers as improper fractions instead of mixed numbers. This avoids any possible confusion between $$2\frac{1}{12}$$ and $$2 \cdot \frac{1}{12}.$$

title: Example 4.52
snippet: Example 4.52: Use a model to find the sum \frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8}. Start with three \frac{1}{8} pieces. Add two \frac{1}{8} pieces. How many \frac{1}{8} pieces are there? There are five \frac{1}{8} pieces, or five-eighths. The model...
body_xml:
Use a model to find the sum $$\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8}.$$ Start with three $$\frac{1}{8}$$ pieces. Add two $$\frac{1}{8}$$ pieces. How many $$\frac{1}{8}$$ pieces are there?
There are five $$\frac{1}{8}$$ pieces, or five-eighths. The model shows that $$\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \frac{5}{8}.$$

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Common Denominators
title: Fraction Addition
snippet: Fraction Addition: If a,b, and c are numbers where c \neq 0, then \frac{a}{c} + \frac{b}{c} = \frac{a + b}{c} To add fractions with a common denominator, add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Fraction Addition" title="Fraction Addition">
    <paragraph>If $$a,b,$$ and $$c$$ are numbers where $$c \neq 0,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{c} + \frac{b}{c} = \frac{a + b}{c}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To add fractions with a common denominator, add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator.</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Find the sum: $$\frac{3}{5} + \frac{1}{5}.$$ $$\frac{3}{5} + \frac{1}{5}$$ Add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. $$\frac{3 + 1}{5}$$ Simplify. $$\frac{4}{5}$$

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Common Denominators
title: Example 4.54
snippet: Example 4.54: Find the sum: \frac{x}{3} + \frac{2}{3}. \frac{x}{3} + \frac{2}{3} Add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. \frac{x + 2}{3} Note that we cannot simplify this fraction any more. Since x and 2 are not...
body_xml:
Find the sum: $$\frac{x}{3} + \frac{2}{3}.$$ $$\frac{x}{3} + \frac{2}{3}$$ Add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. $$\frac{x + 2}{3}$$
Note that we cannot simplify this fraction any more. Since $$x$$ and $$2$$ are not like terms, we cannot combine them.

title: Example 4.55
snippet: Example 4.55: Find the sum: - \frac{9}{d} + \frac{3}{d}. We will begin by rewriting the first fraction with the negative sign in the numerator. - \frac{a}{b} = \frac{- a}{b} - \frac{9}{d} + \frac{3}{d} Rewrite the first fraction with the...
body_xml: Find the sum: $$- \frac{9}{d} + \frac{3}{d}.$$ We will begin by rewriting the first fraction with the negative sign in the numerator. $$- \frac{a}{b} = \frac{- a}{b}$$ $$- \frac{9}{d} + \frac{3}{d}$$ Rewrite the first fraction with the negative in the numerator. $$\frac{-9}{d} + \frac{3}{d}$$ Add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. $$\frac{-9 + 3}{d}$$ Simplify the numerator. $$\frac{-6}{d}$$ Rewrite with negative sign in front of the fraction. $$- \frac{6}{d}$$

title: Example 4.63
snippet: Example 4.63: Find the LCD for the fractions \frac{7}{12} and \frac{5}{18}. Factor each denominator into its primes. List the primes of 12 and the primes of 18 lining them up in columns when possible. Bring down the columns. Multiply the...
body_xml: Find the LCD for the fractions $$\frac{7}{12}$$ and $$\frac{5}{18}.$$ Factor each denominator into its primes. List the primes of 12 and the primes of 18 lining them up in columns when possible. Bring down the columns. Multiply the factors. The product is the LCM. LCM $$= 36$$ The LCM of 12 and 18 is 36, so the LCD of $$\frac{7}{12}$$ and $$\frac{5}{18}$$ is 36. LCD of $$\frac{7}{12}$$ and $$\frac{5}{18}$$ is 36.

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Different Denominators
title: How To
snippet: How To: Find the least common denominator (LCD) of two fractions. Step 1. Factor each denominator into its primes. Step 2. List the primes, matching primes in columns when possible. Step 3. Bring down the columns. Step 4. Multiply the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <heading level="4">Find the least common denominator (LCD) of two fractions.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Factor each denominator into its primes.</item>
      <item>Step 2. List the primes, matching primes in columns when possible.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Bring down the columns.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Multiply the factors. The product is the LCM of the denominators.</item>
      <item>Step 5. The LCM of the denominators is the LCD of the fractions.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="4.64">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the least common denominator for the fractions $$\frac{8}{15}$$ and $$\frac{11}{24}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find the LCD, we find the LCM of the denominators.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Find the LCM of $$15$$ and $$24.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The LCM of $$15$$ and $$24$$ is $$120.$$ So, the LCD of $$\frac{8}{15}$$ and $$\frac{11}{24}$$ is $$120.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Equivalent Fractions Property
snippet: Equivalent Fractions Property: If a,b,c are whole numbers where b \neq 0,c \neq 0, then \frac{a}{b} = \frac{a \cdot c}{b \cdot c} \text{and} \frac{a \cdot c}{b \cdot c} = \frac{a}{b}
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Equivalent Fractions Property" title="Equivalent Fractions Property">
    <paragraph>If $$a,b,c$$ are whole numbers where $$b \neq 0,c \neq 0,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a \cdot c}{b \cdot c} \text{and} \frac{a \cdot c}{b \cdot c} = \frac{a}{b}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Different Denominators
title: Example 4.65
snippet: Example 4.65: Convert \frac{1}{4} and \frac{1}{6} to equivalent fractions with denominator 12, their LCD. Find the LCD. The LCD of \frac{1}{4} and \frac{1}{6} is 12. Find the number to multiply 4 to get 12. Find the number to multiply 6 to...
body_xml:
Convert $$\frac{1}{4}$$ and $$\frac{1}{6}$$ to equivalent fractions with denominator $$12,$$ their LCD. Find the LCD. The LCD of $$\frac{1}{4}$$ and $$\frac{1}{6}$$ is 12. Find the number to multiply 4 to get 12. Find the number to multiply 6 to get 12. Use the Equivalent Fractions Property to convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCD, multiplying both the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same number. Simplify the numerators and denominators.
We do not reduce the resulting fractions. If we did, we would get back to our original fractions and lose the common denominator.

      <item>Step 3. Use the Equivalent Fractions Property to multiply both the numerator and denominator by the number you found in Step 2.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Simplify the numerator and denominator.</item>
    </list>

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Different Denominators
title: Example 4.67
snippet: Example 4.67: Add: \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}. \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} Find the LCD of 2, 3. Change into equivalent fractions with the LCD 6. Simplify the numerators and denominators. \frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6} Add. \frac{5}{6} Remember,...
body_xml:
Add: $$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}.$$ $$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}$$ Find the LCD of 2, 3. Change into equivalent fractions with the LCD 6. Simplify the numerators and denominators. $$\frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6}$$ Add. $$\frac{5}{6}$$
Remember, always check to see if the answer can be simplified. Since $$5$$ and $$6$$ have no common factors, the fraction $$\frac{5}{6}$$ cannot be reduced.

title: Example 4.68
snippet: Example 4.68: Subtract: \frac{1}{2} - \left( {- \frac{1}{4}} \right). \frac{1}{2} - \left( - \frac{1}{4} \right) Find the LCD of 2 and 4. Rewrite as equivalent fractions using the LCD 4. Simplify the first fraction. \frac{2}{4} - \left( -...
body_xml:
Subtract: $$\frac{1}{2} - \left( {- \frac{1}{4}} \right).$$ $$\frac{1}{2} - \left( - \frac{1}{4} \right)$$ Find the LCD of 2 and 4. Rewrite as equivalent fractions using the LCD 4. Simplify the first fraction. $$\frac{2}{4} - \left( - \frac{1}{4} \right)$$ Subtract. $$\frac{2 - (-1)}{4}$$ Simplify. $$\frac{3}{4}$$
One of the fractions already had the least common denominator, so we only had to convert the other fraction.

snippet: Example 4.69: Add: \frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{18}. \frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{18} Find the LCD of 12 and 18. Rewrite as equivalent fractions with the LCD. Simplify the numerators and denominators. \frac{21}{36} + \frac{10}{36} Add. \frac{31}{36}...

Add: $$\frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{18}.$$ $$\frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{18}$$ Find the LCD of 12 and 18. Rewrite as equivalent fractions with the LCD. Simplify the numerators and denominators. $$\frac{21}{36} + \frac{10}{36}$$ Add. $$\frac{31}{36}$$
Because $$31$$ is a prime number, it has no factors in common with $$36.$$ The answer is simplified.

unit_title: Add and Subtract Fractions with Different Denominators
title: Summary of Fraction Operations
snippet: Summary of Fraction Operations: Fraction multiplication: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd} Fraction division: Multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second....
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Summary of Fraction Operations" title="Summary of Fraction Operations">
    <paragraph>Fraction multiplication: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Fraction division: Multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{b} \div \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{d}{c}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Fraction addition: Add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. If the fractions have different denominators, first convert them to equivalent forms with the LCD.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{c} + \frac{b}{c} = \frac{a + b}{c}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Fraction subtraction: Subtract the numerators and place the difference over the common denominator. If the fractions have different denominators, first convert them to equivalent forms with the LCD.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{a}{c} - \frac{b}{c} = \frac{a - b}{c}$$</paragraph>
  </note>
