snippet: Summary of Exponent Properties: If a,b are real numbers and m,n are integers, then \begin{array}{lccl} \textbf{Product Property} & & & {a^{m} \cdot a^{n} = a^{m + n}} \\ \textbf{Power Property} & & & {\left( a^{m} \right)^{n} = a^{m \cdot...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Summary of Exponent Properties" title="Summary of Exponent Properties">
    <paragraph>If $$a,b$$ are real numbers and $$m,n$$ are integers, then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} \textbf{Product Property} & & & {a^{m} \cdot a^{n} = a^{m + n}} \\ \textbf{Power Property} & & & {\left( a^{m} \right)^{n} = a^{m \cdot n}} \\ \textbf{Product to a Power Property} & & & {{(ab)}^{m} = a^{m}b^{m}} \\ \textbf{Quotient Property} & & & {\frac{a^{m}}{a^{n}} = a^{m - n}, a \neq 0} \\ \textbf{Zero Exponent Property} & & & {{a^{0} = 1,} {a \neq 0}} \\ \textbf{Quotient to a Power Property} & & & {\left( \frac{a}{b} \right)^{m} = \frac{a^{m}}{b^{m}}, b \neq 0} \\ \textbf{Definition of Negative Exponent} & & & {a^{- n} = \frac{1}{a^{n}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Scientific Notation
snippet: Scientific Notation: A number is expressed in scientific notation when it is of the form a \times 10^{n} where a \geq 1 and a < 10 and n is an integer.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Scientific Notation" title="Scientific Notation">
    <paragraph>A number is expressed in scientific notation when it is of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a \times 10^{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$a \geq 1$$ and $$a < 10$$ and $$n$$ is an integer.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 10.74
snippet: Example 10.74: Write 37,000 in scientific notation. Step 1: Move the decimal point so that the first factor is greater than or equal to 1 but less than 10. Step 2: Count the number of decimal places, n , that the decimal point was moved....
body_xml: Write $$37,000$$ in scientific notation. Step 1: Move the decimal point so that the first factor is greater than or equal to 1 but less than 10. Step 2: Count the number of decimal places, $$n$$ , that the decimal point was moved. 3.700004 places Step 3: Write the number as a product with a power of 10. $$3.7 \times 10^{4}$$ If the original number is: greater than 1, the power of 10 will be $$10^{n}$$ . between 0 and 1, the power of 10 will be $$10^{-n}$$ Step 4: Check. $$10^{4}$$ is 10,000 and 10,000 times 3.7 will be 37,000. $$37,000 = 3.7 \times 10^{4}$$

body_xml:
Find the greatest common factor of $$24$$ and $$36.$$ Step 1: Factor each coefficient into primes. Write all variables with exponents in expanded form. Factor 24 and 36. Step 2: List all factors--matching common factors in a column. In each column, circle the common factors. Circle the 2, 2, and 3 that are shared by both numbers. Step 3: Bring down the common factors that all expressions share. Bring down the 2, 2, 3 and then multiply. Step 4: Multiply the factors. The GCF of 24 and 36 is 12.
Notice that since the GCF is a factor of both numbers, $$24$$ and $$36$$ can be written as multiples of $$12.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {24 = 12 \cdot 2} \\ {36 = 12 \cdot 3} \end{matrix}$$

body_xml:
<example number="11.2">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Plot $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ in the same rectangular coordinate system.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The coordinate values are the same for both points, but the $$x$$ and $$y$$ values are reversed. Let’s begin with point $$(1,3).$$ The $$x \text{-coordinate}$$ is $$1$$ so find $$1$$ on the $$x \text{-axis}$$ and sketch a vertical line through $$x = 1.$$ The $$y \text{-coordinate}$$ is $$3$$ so we find $$3$$ on the $$y \text{-axis}$$ and sketch a horizontal line through $$y = 3.$$ Where the two lines meet, we plot the point $$(1,3).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To plot the point $$(3,1),$$ we start by locating $$3$$ on the $$x \text{-axis}$$ and sketch a vertical line through $$x = 3.$$ Then we find $$1$$ on the $$y \text{-axis}$$ and sketch a horizontal line through $$y = 1.$$ Where the two lines meet, we plot the point $$(3,1).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the order of the coordinates does matter, so, $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ is not the same point as $$\left( {3,1} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="11.3">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Plot each point in the rectangular coordinate system and identify the quadrant in which the point is located:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$(-1,3)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$(-3,-4)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$(2,-3)$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left( 3,\frac{5}{2} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first number of the coordinate pair is the $$x \text{-coordinate} ,$$ and the second number is the $$y \text{-coordinate} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓐ Since $$x = -1,y = 3,$$ the point $$\left( {-1,3} \right)$$ is in Quadrant II.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ Since $$x = -3,y = -4,$$ the point $$\left( {-3,-4} \right)$$ is in Quadrant III.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒ Since $$x = 2,y = -1,$$ the point $$(2,-1)$$ is in Quadrant lV.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓓ Since $$x = 3,y = \frac{5}{2},$$ the point $$\left( {3,\frac{5}{2}} \right)$$ is in Quadrant I. It may be helpful to write $$\frac{5}{2}$$ as the mixed number, $$2\frac{1}{2},$$ or decimal, $$2.5.$$ Then we know that the point is halfway between $$2$$ and $$3$$ on the $$y \text{-axis} .$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Example 11.12

We can substitute any value we want for $$x\$$ or any value for $$y.$$ Let's pick $$x = 0.$$ What is the value of $$y\$$ if $$x = 0$$ ? Step 2: Substitute that value into the equation. Solve for the other variable. Substitute $$0$$ for $$x.$$ Simplify. Divide both sides by 2. Step 3: Write the solution as an ordered pair. So, when $$x = 0,y = 3.$$ This solution is represented by the ordered pair $$(0,3).$$ Step 4: Check. Is the result a true equation? Yes!

<example number="11.29">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the most convenient method to graph each line:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$y = -3\$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$4x-6y = 12\$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x = 2\$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$y = \frac{2}{5}x-1$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$y = -3$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This equation has only one variable, $$y.$$ Its graph is a horizontal line crossing the $$y \text{-axis}$$ at $$-3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ $$4x-6y = 12$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This equation is of the form $${Ax + By = C}.$$ Find the intercepts and one more point.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒ $$x = 2$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There is only one variable, $$x.$$ The graph is a vertical line crossing the $$x \text{-axis}$$ at $$2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓓ $$y = \frac{2}{5}x-1$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$y$$ is isolated on the left side of the equation, it will be easiest to graph this line by plotting three points.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Slope of a line

    <paragraph>The slope of a line is $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rise measures the vertical change and the run measures the horizontal change.</paragraph>

title: Example 11.32
snippet: Example 11.32: Use a geoboard to model a line with slope \frac{1}{2}. To model a line with a specific slope on a geoboard, we need to know the rise and the run. Use the slope formula. m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } Replace m with...
body_xml:
Use a geoboard to model a line with slope $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ To model a line with a specific slope on a geoboard, we need to know the rise and the run. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Replace $$m$$ with $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . $$\frac{1}{2} = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$
So, the rise is $$1$$ unit and the run is $$2$$ units. Start at a peg in the lower left of the geoboard. Stretch the rubber band up $$1$$ unit, and then right $$2$$ units. The hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the rubber band represents a line with a slope of $$\frac{1}{2}.$$

title: Example 11.33
snippet: Example 11.33: Use a geoboard to model a line with slope \frac{-1}{4}, Use the slope formula. m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } Replace m with -\frac{1}{4} . -\frac{1}{4} = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } So, the rise is -1 and the...
body_xml:
Use a geoboard to model a line with slope $$\frac{-1}{4},$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Replace $$m$$ with $$-\frac{1}{4}$$ . $$-\frac{1}{4} = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$
So, the rise is $$-1$$ and the run is $$4.$$ Since the rise is negative, we choose a starting peg on the upper left that will give us room to count down. We stretch the rubber band down $$1$$ unit, then to the right $$4$$ units. The hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the rubber band represents a line whose slope is $$- \frac{1}{4}.$$

title: Example 11.34
snippet: Example 11.34: Find the slope of the line shown: Locate two points on the graph, choosing points whose coordinates are integers. We will use (0,-3) and (5,1). Starting with the point on the left, (0,-3), sketch a right triangle, going from...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line shown: Locate two points on the graph, choosing points whose coordinates are integers. We will use $$(0,-3)$$ and $$(5,1).$$ Starting with the point on the left, $$(0,-3),$$ sketch a right triangle, going from the first point to the second point, $$(5,1).$$ Count the rise on the vertical leg of the triangle. The rise is 4 units. Count the run on the horizontal leg. The run is 5 units. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{4}{5}$$ The slope of the line is $$\frac{4}{5}$$ .
Notice that the slope is positive since the line slants upward from left to right.

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">

    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Locate two points on the line whose coordinates are integers.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Starting with the point on the left, sketch a right triangle, with the hypotenuse going from the first point to the second point.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Count the rise and the run on the legs of the triangle.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Take the ratio of rise to run to find the slope. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$</item>

title: Example 11.35
snippet: Example 11.35: Find the slope of the line shown: Locate two points on the graph. Look for points with coordinates that are integers. We can choose any points, but we will use (0, 5) and (3, 3). Starting with the point on the left, sketch a...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line shown: Locate two points on the graph. Look for points with coordinates that are integers. We can choose any points, but we will use (0, 5) and (3, 3). Starting with the point on the left, sketch a right triangle, with the hypotenuse going from the first point to the second point. Count the rise – it is negative. The rise is −2. Count the run. The run is 3. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{-2}{3}$$ Simplify. $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ The slope of the line is $$- \frac{2}{3}.$$
Notice that the slope is negative since the line slants downward from left to right. What if we had chosen different points? Let’s find the slope of the line again, this time using different points. We will use the points $$(-3,7)$$ and $$(6,1).$$ Starting at $$(-3,7),$$ sketch a right triangle to $$(6,1).$$ Count the rise. The rise is −6. Count the run. The run is 9. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{-6}{9}$$ Simplify the fraction. $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ The slope of the line is $$- \frac{2}{3}.$$
It does not matter which points you use—the slope of the line is always the same. The slope of a line is constant!

title: Slope Formula
snippet: Slope Formula: The slope of the line between two points (x_{1},y_{1}) and (x_{2},y_{2}) is m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Slope Formula" title="Slope Formula">
    <paragraph>The slope of the line between two points $$(x_{1},y_{1})$$ and $$(x_{2},y_{2})$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 11.38
snippet: Example 11.38: Find the slope of the line between the points \left( {1,2} \right) and \left( {4,5} \right). We’ll call (1,2) point #1 and (4,5) point #2. \overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{\left( {1,2} \right)} \text{and} \overset{x_{2},y_{2}}{\left(...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line between the points $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {4,5} \right).$$ We’ll call $$(1,2)$$ point #1 and $$(4,5)$$ point #2. $$\overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{\left( {1,2} \right)} \text{and} \overset{x_{2},y_{2}}{\left( {4,5} \right)}$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ Substitute the values in the slope formula: $$y\$$ of the second point minus $$y\$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{5 - 2}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ $$x\$$ of the second point minus $$x\$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{5 - 2}{4 - 1}$$ Simplify the numerator and the denominator. $$m = \frac{3}{3}$$ $$m = 1$$
Let’s confirm this by counting out the slope on the graph. The rise is $$3$$ and the run is $$3,$$ so $$\begin{array}{l} \\ {m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }} \\ {m = \frac{3}{3}} \\ {m = 1} \end{array}$$

title: Example 11.39
snippet: Example 11.39: Find the slope of the line through the points \left( {-2,-3} \right) and \left( {-7,4} \right). We’ll call (-2,-3) point #1 and (-7,4) point #2. \overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{\left( {-2,-3} \right)} \text{and}...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line through the points $$\left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-7,4} \right).$$ We’ll call $$(-2,-3)$$ point #1 and $$(-7,4)$$ point #2. $$\overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{\left( {-2,-3} \right)} \text{and} \overset{x_{2},y_{2}}{\left( {-7,4} \right)}$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ Substitute the values $$y\$$ of the second point minus $$y\$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{4 - (-3)}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ $$x\$$ of the second point minus $$x\$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{4 - (-3)}{-7 - (-2)}$$ Simplify. $$m = \frac{7}{-5}$$ $$m = - \frac{7}{5}$$
Let’s confirm this on the graph shown. $$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ \\ { m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }} \\ {m = \frac{-7}{5}} \\ { m = - \frac{7}{5}} \end{matrix}$$

title: Example 11.40
snippet: Example 11.40: Graph the line passing through the point \left( {1,-1} \right) whose slope is m = \frac{3}{4}. Plot the given point, \left( {1,-1} \right). Use the slope formula m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } to identify the rise...
body_xml:
<example number="11.40">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Graph the line passing through the point $$\left( {1,-1} \right)$$ whose slope is $$m = \frac{3}{4}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Plot the given point, $$\left( {1,-1} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the slope formula $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ to identify the rise and the run.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ { m = \frac{3}{4}} \\ {\frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } = \frac{3}{4}} \\ \\ \\ { \text{rise} = 3} \\ { \text{run} = 4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Starting at the point we plotted, count out the rise and run to mark the second point. We count $$3$$ units up and $$4$$ units right.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we connect the points with a line and draw arrows at the ends to show it continues.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can check our line by starting at any point and counting up $$3$$ and to the right $$4.$$ We should get to another point on the line.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 11.43
snippet: Example 11.43: The pitch of a building’s roof is the slope of the roof. Knowing the pitch is important in climates where there is heavy snowfall. If the roof is too flat, the weight of the snow may cause it to collapse. What is the slope...
body_xml: The pitch of a building’s roof is the slope of the roof. Knowing the pitch is important in climates where there is heavy snowfall. If the roof is too flat, the weight of the snow may cause it to collapse. What is the slope of the roof shown? Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values for rise and run. $$m = \frac{ \text{9 ft} }{ \text{18 ft} }$$ Simplify. $$m = \frac{1}{2}$$ The slope of the roof is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ .

title: Example 11.44
snippet: Example 11.44: Sewage pipes must slope down \frac{1}{4} inch per foot in order to drain properly. What is the required slope? Use the slope formula. m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{in} .}{1 \text{ft} }...
body_xml: Sewage pipes must slope down $$\frac{1}{4}$$ inch per foot in order to drain properly. What is the required slope? Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ $$m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{in} .}{1 \text{ft} }$$ $$m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{in} .}{1 \text{ft} }$$ Convert 1 foot to 12 inches. $$m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{in} .}{12 \text{in.} }$$ Simplify. $$m = - \frac{1}{48}$$ The slope of the pipe is $$- \frac{1}{48}.$$
